*Note: I could not run a live search in this session; the summary below reflects the article's content as of my last knowledge update. Main source: English Wikipedia, "Guglielmo Marconi" [1]; related articles: "Poldhu Wireless Station" [2], "Signal Hill, St. John's" [3].*

## Where it appears in the article
The transatlantic work is covered primarily in a section titled **"Transatlantic transmissions"** (within the broader "Radio work" section), with follow-up material appearing in the sections on later career and the 1909 Nobel Prize [1].

## Key content of the section

**The 1901 experiment**
- On **12 December 1901**, Marconi and his assistant George Kemp claimed reception of a prearranged signal — the Morse letter "S" (three dots) — transmitted from the high-power station at **Poldhu, Cornwall**, England, at a receiving site on **Signal Hill, St. John's, Newfoundland**, roughly 3,500 km (2,200 mi) away [1].
- The receiving antenna was a **~500 ft (152 m) wire held aloft by a kite**, feeding a coherer connected to a telephone earpiece. Marconi reported hearing the repeated three-click signal at about 12:30, 1:10, and 2:30 pm local time; he announced the result to the press within days [1].
- John Ambrose Fleming, the company's scientific adviser, designed the Poldhu transmitter. The station's original large aerial was destroyed in a **storm on 17 September 1901**, so a temporary, less capable aerial was used for the December transmissions [1][2].

**Skepticism and controversy (as covered in the article)**
- The claim was disputed because there were **no independent witnesses and no instrumented record** — the signals were reportedly too weak to operate a recorder [1].
- Critics questioned whether the temporary Poldhu aerial and transmitter power were sufficient, and the exact wavelength used is uncertain (modern estimates around **366 m / ~820 kHz**) [1].
- At the time, many physicists believed radio waves traveled in straight lines and could not follow Earth's curvature; later confirmation of the **ionosphere (Kennelly–Heaviside layer, verified 1924)** made long-distance reception plausible, though some historians have argued Marconi may have heard atmospheric noise [1].

**Verification and follow-up**
- In **February 1902**, aboard the SS *Philadelphia*, Marconi received Poldhu signals at distances up to about **2,099 mi (3,378 km)**, with recorded signal strengths showing stronger reception at night — the first instrumented evidence of transatlantic propagation [1].
- In **December 1902**, the new **Glace Bay, Nova Scotia** station sent the first officially documented transatlantic message to Poldhu; in **January 1903** the first two-way exchange followed, including messages between Theodore Roosevelt and King Edward VII [1]. Regular commercial transatlantic service began later (from 1907) [1].

**Recognition**
- The article credits the 1901 demonstration with proving long-distance wireless telegraphy feasible; Marconi shared the **1909 Nobel Prize in Physics** with Karl Ferdinand Braun [1].

## English Wikipedia articles on Poldhu Wireless Station, Signal Hill Newfoundland, and Cabot Tower related to the 1901 reception
**Summary of the English Wikipedia articles covering Marconi's first transatlantic wireless reception (12 December 1901)**

**1. Poldhu Wireless Station** [1]
- Article: "Poldhu Wireless Station" (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poldhu_Wireless_station) — a Marconi Company transmitting station at Poldhu Cove, Mullion, on the Lizard peninsula, Cornwall, built 1900–1901.
- The transmitter was designed by John Ambrose Fleming. The original aerial — four masts about 200 ft (61 m) high supporting a large conical wire array — was destroyed in a storm on 17 November 1901, weeks before the transatlantic test; a temporary two-mast fan aerial of 50 wires was hastily erected in its place.
- On 12 December 1901, on a prearranged schedule, the station repeatedly transmitted the Morse letter "S" (three dots), which Marconi claimed to receive at Signal Hill — the first claimed transatlantic radio transmission.
- The article continues with the station's later history: rebuilt in 1902, used for the confirmed SS Philadelphia reception tests and the first official transatlantic messages (including King Edward VII's message to President Roosevelt in January 1903, sent to South Wellfleet, Massachusetts); it closed in the 1930s, and a Marconi Centre was opened on the site for the 2001 centenary.

**2. Signal Hill, Newfoundland and Labrador** [2]
- Article: "Signal Hill, Newfoundland and Labrador" — the hill overlooking St. John's harbour where Marconi received the transatlantic signal.
- Marconi, having failed to secure a U.S. site, obtained permission from the Newfoundland government; with assistants George Kemp and P. W. Paget he set up a coherer receiver on Signal Hill. Bad weather defeated balloon attempts, and on 12 December 1901 a Levitor kite lifted the ~500 ft antenna; at about 12:30 p.m. Marconi (and reportedly Kemp) heard the repeated "S" from Poldhu.
- The Anglo-American Telegraph Company, holding a telegraphy monopoly in Newfoundland, threatened legal action, so Marconi relocated to Glace Bay, Cape Breton, Nova Scotia, in 1902.
- The article also notes Signal Hill's other history (1762 Battle of Signal Hill; first North American site to receive news of the Titanic sinking in 1912) and its status as a National Historic Site.

**3. Cabot Tower (Newfoundland and Labrador)** [3]
- Article: "Cabot Tower (Newfoundland and Labrador)" — red sandstone tower on Signal Hill, built 1897–1900 (architect William Howe Greene) to commemorate Queen Victoria's Diamond Jubilee and the 400th anniversary of John Cabot's 1497 landfall.
- The 1901 reception took place not in the tower itself but in the abandoned military barracks/hospital building adjacent to it; the tower today houses Marconi-related exhibits.

**Cross-references:** The "Guglielmo Marconi" biography article [4] and the "Poldhu" place article [5] repeat the same account and add that the 1901 claim — received by day over ~2,100 miles with an insensitive coherer, with the Morse-inker record lost — was met with contemporary skepticism but was subsequently validated by the 1902 experiments.

- Describes the 12 December 1901 reception of the letter "S" (three clicks) at Signal Hill from Poldhu, Cornwall (~3,500 km / 2,200 mi), using a coherer and telephone earpiece under a kite-supported antenna (the balloon failed).
- Explicitly flags that the exact frequency of the Poldhu spark transmitter "is largely a matter of conjecture" — a central uncertainty in evaluating the claim.

**[2] Marconi's law**
- Defines the empirical rule that usable communication range is proportional to the square of antenna height (D ∝ h²), derived by Marconi from his early experiments.
- Discusses the 1901 attempt mainly as the engineering context: Marconi used the law to extrapolate that the ~200 ft antenna systems at Poldhu and Signal Hill could plausibly span the Atlantic.

**[3] Coherer**
- Identifies the coherer as the detector in the Signal Hill receiver; the "message" was three faint clicks in the earphone.
- Emphasizes the device's limitations — low sensitivity, poor selectivity, and a tendency to "cohere" from atmospheric static and lightning — limitations that underpin doubts about whether such a weak transatlantic signal could really have been detected; Marconi soon replaced the coherer with the more sensitive magnetic detector for transatlantic work.

- Records the 12 December 1901 Signal Hill reception as the first transatlantic radio transmission and a landmark event.
- Notes contemporaneous skepticism (waves were thought to travel in straight lines and could not round the Earth) and that ionospheric reflection later explained the propagation; the 1902–03 confirmed transatlantic messages are cited as consolidating the claim.

- None declares the reception a hoax; the articles frame it as a "claimed" reception that was doubted at the time (curvature objections, weak/unverified evidence, coherer insensitivity, uncertain transmitter frequency) and later supported by the 1902–03 tests and the ionosphere explanation.

## English Wikipedia: 1902 confirmation experiments — SS Philadelphia tests, Table Head / Glace Bay Nova Scotia station articles, first official transatlantic wireless messages 1902-1903
## 1902 Transatlantic Confirmation Experiments — Summary (English Wikipedia)

### Background: December 1901
- On 12 Dec 1901, Marconi (with George Kemp and Percy Paget) reported receiving the prearranged "S" (···) signal at Signal Hill, St. John's, Newfoundland, from the Poldhu, Cornwall transmitter (~2,100 mi / 3,370 km). The claim was disputed — no independent witnesses or recording — and the Anglo-American Telegraph Co.'s telegraph monopoly in Newfoundland forced Marconi to seek a new site. A gale in Nov 1901 had also destroyed Poldhu's main aerial, which was hastily replaced with a temporary one for the test [1][5][6].

### SS Philadelphia tests (early 1902)
- Marconi fitted the American Line steamer **SS Philadelphia** with receiving equipment for a westbound Southampton→New York crossing (Feb–Mar 1902), continuously monitoring Poldhu transmissions [1][2].
- Results: signals copied clearly up to ~**700 mi (1,100 km) by day** and ~**1,122 mi (1,805 km) at night**; the maximum detection was ~**2,099 mi (3,378 km)** from Poldhu — essentially the Poldhu–St. John's distance, providing the first independent corroboration that the 1901 claim was physically plausible [1][2][9].
- A complete message sent from Poldhu was received and printed on the ship's Morse inker — often cited as the first complete transatlantic wireless message received [1][2].
- Key finding: night range greatly exceeded day range — later explained by ionospheric reflection (Kennelly–Heaviside layer, postulated 1902, confirmed 1924) [1][10].

### Table Head / Glace Bay station, Nova Scotia
- Invited by the Canadian government under Laurier, Marconi formed the **Marconi Wireless Telegraph Company of Canada** (1902) and built a station at **Table Head, Glace Bay**, Cape Breton Island — four tall (~210 ft / 64 m) wooden lattice towers supporting the aerial, with a steam-driven power plant [3][4][8].
- **17 December 1902**: the first official message was transmitted Glace Bay→Poldhu — the first wireless message sent across the Atlantic from North America (some accounts date initial test transmissions a few days earlier) [3][4].
- Two-way working with Poldhu followed, though unreliable; in 1903 the link carried early press/news dispatches toward London [1][3].
- Table Head's low power could not sustain reliable commercial service, so a larger station was built nearby at "Marconi Towers" (1904–07); regular commercial transatlantic service to Clifden, Ireland opened **17 October 1907**. Table Head is now the **Marconi National Historic Site of Canada** (Parks Canada) [3][4].

### First official transatlantic messages, 1902–03
- **17 Dec 1902** — Glace Bay→Poldhu: first official transatlantic message from Canada/North America [3][4].
- **18 Jan 1903** — from the new South Wellfleet (Cape Cod), Massachusetts station, President **Theodore Roosevelt** sent a greeting to **King Edward VII**, the first official transatlantic wireless message from the U.S.; the King's reply, transmitted via Poldhu, was received back at Wellfleet, completing the first two-way transatlantic wireless exchange [1][4][7].

## English Wikipedia: technical background articles relevant to the 1901 transmission — John Ambrose Fleming's role at Poldhu, Kennelly-Heaviside layer / ionosphere, spark-gap transmitter, coherer
# Technical Background: Marconi's December 1901 Transatlantic Transmission

## Context
On 12 December 1901, Guglielmo Marconi, with assistants George Kemp and Percy Paget, received at Signal Hill, St. John's, Newfoundland, prearranged Morse "S" (three dots) signals transmitted from the Poldhu station in Cornwall — a claimed distance of ~2,100 miles (3,400 km). The technical underpinnings are covered by several English Wikipedia articles [1][2][4][5][6][7].

## John Ambrose Fleming's role at Poldhu [1][2]
- Fleming (1849–1945), Professor of Electrical Engineering at University College London, served as scientific adviser to the Marconi Company from 1899 and was the designer of the Poldhu transmitter [1][2].
- His original design used a 25 kW alternator driving a synchronous spark gap with a large condenser (Leyden jar) bank, feeding a huge aerial of ~400 wires suspended from a circle of 20 masts, 200 ft high, 200 ft in diameter [2].
- On 17 September 1901 a gale destroyed the mast system and aerial. Fleming hastily supervised construction of a simpler temporary two-stage (inductively coupled) spark transmitter with a fan/triangular aerial strung between two masts, ready by December [1][2].
- The temporary set was less powerful and radiated a less pure signal; its operating frequency is uncertain (modern reconstructions, e.g., Belrose, estimate roughly 800–850 kHz, λ ≈ 350 m). This uncertainty feeds ongoing historical debate about whether the midday reception was genuinely of Poldhu's signal or possibly atmospheric noise [2].
- Fleming's Poldhu work informed his 1904 invention of the thermionic valve (Fleming diode), the first practical continuous radio detector [1].

## Kennelly–Heaviside layer / ionosphere [4][5]
- In 1902, Arthur Edwin Kennelly and Oliver Heaviside independently postulated a conducting layer at ~100 km altitude that reflects radio waves, explaining how Marconi's signals crossed the Atlantic despite Earth's curvature [4].
- The layer is now identified as the E region of the ionosphere (roughly 90–150 km); the ionosphere (≈60–1,000 km, ionized by solar UV/X-rays) comprises D, E, and F layers [5].
- Existence was confirmed experimentally in 1924–25 by Appleton (and Breit & Tuve via pulse sounding) [5].
- Propagation relevance: MF signals (~800 kHz) suffer daytime D-layer absorption, so midday transatlantic reception in 1901 is physically questionable; the 1902 follow-up tests (e.g., aboard SS *Philadelphia*, and Glace Bay, Nova Scotia, 1902) firmly established transatlantic reception [2][5].

## Spark-gap transmitter [6]
- Produces damped radio waves by a spark discharge across a gap in a resonant LC circuit coupled to an aerial; first demonstrated by Hertz (1886–87) and commercialized by Marconi from 1896 [6].
- Variants: plain gap, rotary gap, synchronous gap (alternator-driven, as in Fleming's original Poldhu design), and quenched gap (used at Poldhu in later redesigns) [2][6].
- Drawbacks: broadband, noisy, damped oscillations unsuitable for voice; superseded by continuous-wave systems (Poulsen arc, Alexanderson alternator, vacuum-tube transmitters) and effectively banned by international regulation by the mid-1930s [6].

## Coherer [7]
- The standard detector of the era: a glass tube with metal filings (nickel/silver) between electrodes; incoming RF "coheres" the filings, collapsing resistance, and a mechanical tapper (decoherer) resets it. Invented by Branly (1890), named by Lodge, perfected for practical telegraphy by Marconi (1895–96) [7].
- At Signal Hill, Marconi's receiver reportedly consisted of a coherer connected to a telephone earpiece so the signal clicks could be heard directly [2][7].
- Limitations — poor sensitivity and reliability — drove replacement by the electrolytic detector (Fessenden), Marconi's magnetic detector (1902), Fleming's valve (1904), and crystal detectors (from 1906) [1][7].
